newsitem.title: INDIA: Security-conscious India lets down its guard.
newsitem.headline: Security-conscious India lets down its guard.

text.p: Under pressure from irate citizens, the Indian government on Thursday announced it was scaling back "obtrusive" security for public officials which often ends up forcing roads and even airports to shut down.
The government said in a statement that it was revising the system to make "VVIP/VIP security less obtrusive, less irritating and less inconvenient".

Known as VIPs (very important persons) or VVIPs (very, very important persons), senior public officials are commonly surrounded by armed bodyguards who sleep in sprawling tents outside the authorities' homes.
The officials travel in large convoys, and hundreds of police are needed to close off roads and highways whenever the prime minister travels, causing traffic headaches.
All airport traffic is put on hold when the prime minister's plane takes off or lands.
VIP security grew to huge proportions during the 1980s, when India saw a rise in Sikh and Kashmiri separatist violence and its army helped Sri Lanka combat Tamil Tiger guerrillas.

The then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was shot dead in 1984 by Sikh bodyguards opposed to her move to send the army into a holy Sikh shrine used by separatists. In 1991, her son Rajiv was assassinated by a female Tamil suicide bomber.

The government said that effective immediately, only one lane will be closed when the prime minister's car passes. Shops will not be forced shut as a rule, and pedestrians will not be told "to freeze or face the other side", it said.
The number of policemen would be cut to a fraction of the current deployment, and traffic will not be held up for more than three minutes.

The number of ministers and officers who see the prime minister off at the airport will be limited, and no one will have to come for domestic trips. Air space and air traffic will no longer be closed for his flights.
The government will cut back the number of guards for senior officials, and unless there is a specific threat, public servants will pay at least half the cost of the protection.
People out of office will have to pay the full cost.
